articles.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
articles.snippet: Ukraine's president voices frustration with US and says it is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks to end the war.
articles.full_text:
Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.
Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
- Published7 days ago
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
- Published6 days ago
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them moreâ¦ It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink â and its military version, Starshield â were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

articles.title: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter
articles.snippet: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
articles.full_text:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.
Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.
The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.
The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?
Surviving blackouts
Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.
Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.
I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.
Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
Raving through the war
I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.
We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.
Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% â way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.
What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.
Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method â sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.
Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia â "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a cafÃ© here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.
It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.
There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.
How does it all end?
The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.
So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.
But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.
Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.
And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."
Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (Â£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.
Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.
At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.
The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: 'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
articles.snippet: Stormy weather in New York City prompted organisers to push back the Macy's parade by two days - leaving some musicians stuck.
articles.full_text:
'We couldn't give up that easily': Marching bands scramble to cover costs after Thanksgiving parade rearranged
- Published
Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (Â£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.
Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
- Published1 day ago
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
"We have a lot to be thankful for this Thanksgiving."
Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the NÄ Koa AliÊ»i HawaiÊ»i All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC earlier on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
But the musicians sprang into action quickly, he said. "We come from a very far place," Badua said, adding that "to get so close to the finish line and not show up for it, we couldn't give up that easily".
The response from friends and family had been "incredible", he said.
Badua was hopeful his group would have the same experience he had when he first performed at the parade in 2003, as student drum major.
"The energy is palpable, people are just excited to see a band that is great."
Another musical act, from Illinois, told the BBC on Thursday it was trying to raise $175,000 to cover another night in a hotel, additional food, and bus costs back to the city of Champaign.
"Things are going well due to the very generous support of so many amazing human beings," said Professor Barry Houser, director of the University of Illinois Marching Illini.
While awaiting the parade, musicians and punters alike have sheltered from the heavy wind and rain brought by the storm to eastern areas of the US.
Hundreds of thousands of homes were without power in the storm's aftermath Friday, and coastal areas had flooded. The National Weather Service (NWS) expects conditions to improve gradually on Friday.
Additional reporting by Jessica Murphy

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
articles.snippet: Paul Mackenzie is found guilty of killing his followers, weeks after being jailed for the mass murder of children.
articles.full_text:
Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted over further 123 deaths
- Published
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.
The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
Earlier this week, Mackenzie was also convicted of:
assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
engaging in organised criminal activity
radicalisation
facilitating the commission of a terrorist act
being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
- Published19 October
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Post-mortem records showed many of the victims had died of starvation while the remains of others were mostly skeletal, making the establishment of their cause of death impossible.
Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he had lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie.
"I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court last month.
"All six of my children died in Shakahola forest. I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel."
The deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.
Additional reporting by Thomas Mukhwana

articles.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
articles.snippet: The struggle many face in buying a home has been the biggest issue of a bitter campaign.
articles.full_text:
Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
- Published
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.
The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace SÃ¡nchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.
Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
- Published6 hours ago
Who to watch in Spain's election race
- Published7 hours ago
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
- Published2 days ago
Sparking the protests in September was the eviction â and subsequent death in hospital â of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal (no relation to Santiago). She could not afford a tripling of her rent in Madrid.
But it is Spain's third city, Valencia, that is at the heart of what many call a full-blown housing crisis.
"We want to live together but we look at the prices of property and it's impossible," says 25-year-old Nuria Cifuentes from the city.
She and her boyfriend Miguel MartÃnez work as sports journalists but are still living with their respective families because of the high cost of renting a flat, even with their combined salaries.
"Half of what we earn would go on rent of more than â¬1,000 a month," Miguel, 26, says.
We meet the couple outside Valencia's futuristic science museum, whose distinctive design is often compared to the skeleton of a whale.
This coastal location has witnessed the biggest rise in rent prices of any major Spanish city over the past half a decade, according to official data from the INE, the national statistics office.
One study from the city's Polytechnic University put the increase at 78% between 2020 and 2025.
SÃ¡nchez called a snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.
A revised version was later pushed through a parliamentary standing committee â restricting evictions and capping rent rises â but opponents say he has had eight years to sort the problem and has resolutely failed.
Nuria and Miguel say the soaring cost of housing means that life is on pause for them, as they're unable to make concrete plans for the future.
"Maybe we want to have kids, maybe we want to actually buy somewhere, but there are so many unknowns that all I see is a black expanse," Nuria says.
"The problem here is that our salaries are very low and life is very expensive."
The wider cost of living is the second most important issue for Spaniards, according to numerous surveys carried out during this election period.
Wages failing to catch up with rising prices â despite Spain's GDP growing faster than the three bigger EU countries, Germany, France and Italy â is another reason why SÃ¡nchez's PSOE party is only sitting in second place, according to final opinion polls.
FeijÃ³o is said to be most likely to form the next government with the support of Vox under its leader Santiago Abascal.
Having called access to housing a "vital emergency", FeijÃ³o wants to cut taxes for under-40s buying their first home and scrap the Socialists' housing law.
On housing, Vox has gone further than PSOE and PP, promising to prioritise Spaniards over foreigners for social housing and housing aid, as well as other welfare benefits.
On immigration, identified as the third most important issue, Vox advocates deportations for criminals from abroad and, most controversially, a policy of remigration for foreign nationals who "do not contribute to Spain".
Opponents of Vox say those who have arrived legally and live and work peacefully risk being forced out.
But 30-year-old Daniel, who is currently unemployed, says he is ready to give his vote to Vox for the first time.
"First of all, it's immigration. It's bad in Spain today â that's why I'm going further to the right," he says.
"The left helps those who don't work, but we need people who work and contribute. We need to give less aid to people who come from abroad and don't contribute."
Daniel says taxes need to come down immediately.
"We are almost being charged to just breathe at the moment," he says.
We meet Daniel coming out of a shopping centre. We explain that other people we met in the previous hour who told us they support Vox did not want to give their name or be photographed.
Is he proud to be voting far right, or does he have concerns about his choice?
"I'll say it like it isâ¦ I've always been centre right but have gone to the extreme rightâ¦ I've decided to choose nationalism."
Spain's control of its borders was criticised by 22 of its 26 EU partners in the summer, in a rebuke to SÃ¡nchez.
In July more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in just two days.
Vox called it an "invasion".
SÃ¡nchez has argued the foreign workforce is essential to Spain's economic growth, and in April announced plans to give half a million undocumented migrants legal status.
In the final days of the campaign, SÃ¡nchez has made a flurry of new spending announcements amounting to billions of euros, promising wage rises in the public sector, higher pensions and discounted transport.
Twenty-year-old student MarÃa GarcÃa says she welcomes the promises but asks why they have come so late in the day.
"The Socialist party have been in power for eight years and now suddenly, during the election campaign, they are passing a lot of progressive laws â which I agree with â but isn't that hypocritical?" she says.
"I don't really have a choice but to vote for them, but come on â you had eight years to do all this!"
Maria's sentiments chime with those of her boyfriend German Martinez, 18.
I put it to them that nearly a fifth of Spaniards are said to be choosing Vox and a number of studies say it's set to be the top choice of first-time voters.
MarÃa shakes her head.
"I believe Spain is stepping into the lion's den because we are scared of the dogs outside. We need to be careful," she says.
"People need to inform themselves â just listen to what these guys say. That 20% of Spanish people agree with them really scares me."
SÃ¡nchez will be hoping that fear among the undecided of a national government that includes Vox will save him.
He is a great political survivor, but even if his party wins the most votes he has no obvious path to build a majority.

articles.title: Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
articles.snippet: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
articles.full_text:
Brazil pushes back on Macron calling its meat 'doped'
- Published
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".
France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.
In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".
Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.
In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at ÃlysÃ©e Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.
"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".
Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (Â£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

articles.title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
articles.snippet: The former Murdoch media executive was overheard at an event referring to the way Grace Tame was dressed.
articles.full_text:
Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
- Published
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.
Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.
"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"
From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

articles.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.snippet: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
articles.full_text:
Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
- Published
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.
Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."
The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.
On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.
The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.
Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill
- Published46 minutes ago
Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laÃ¯citÃ© - as a core component of its identity.
Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc QuÃ©bÃ©cois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.
"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-FranÃ§ois Blanchet told reporters in French.

Mexico files complaint with US over DEA tip line on alleged drug dealers
Tensions rise over DEA tip line, with Mexico emphasising respect for its sovereignty amidst growing bilateral discord.
Mexico has filed a formal complaint with the United States over a US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) tip line seeking information on suspected drug traffickers and alleged corruption among Mexican officials, President Claudia Sheinbaum has announced, touching on a particularly sensitive issue in bilateral relations.
Foreign Minister Juan Ramon de la Fuente contacted the US ambassador to Mexico to lodge the complaint, Sheinbaum said on Friday during her morning news conference, adding that the ambassador said he would look into the issue.

- list 3 of 3Mexico seeks US talks about suspected SpaceX debris
Alleged links between elected officials and organised crime have become an increasingly fraught issue for Sheinbaum’s government, which has rejected what it describes as attempts by US authorities to interfere in Mexican affairs.
“We have made it very clear that our relationship with the United States is one of coordination, not subordination,” Sheinbaum said.
The complaint comes despite a significant expansion of security cooperation between the two nations under Sheinbaum. Her government has stepped up efforts against organised crime and fentanyl trafficking amid pressure from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly threatened unilateral action against Mexican cartels if Mexico did not do more.
On Thursday, Sheinbaum in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press news agency revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the southwestern US with deadly drugs.
“The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot,” Sheinbaum said. “The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organised crime, or what they call terrorist groups.”
Recent cooperation has included the capture of drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro“, in an operation Mexican officials said was carried out by Mexican troops supported by US intelligence.
Bilateral security cooperation, however, has been repeatedly tested. The DEA has long been a source of friction, with Mexican officials accusing the agency of overstepping its authority and infringing on national sovereignty.
Tensions also flared earlier this year after two US officials who were killed in the northern state of Chihuahua were identified by sources as CIA personnel, exposing US intelligence activities that Sheinbaum said her government was not aware of.
The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment by the Reuters news agency on the Mexican complaint.
The US agency this week announced a tip line seeking information on alleged members of criminal organisations, corrupt officials and others collaborating with drug traffickers in Sinaloa, the northwestern Mexican state that is the stronghold of the Sinaloa Cartel.
“Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter,” DEA Administrator Terry Cole said in a post on social media, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.
The tip line comes amid broader US pressure on Mexico over suspected links between politicians and cartels.
Reuters reported in June that the Trump administration had pressed Mexico to investigate politicians suspected of cartel links and extradite them to the US to face criminal charges. Those discussions included allegations involving figures from Sheinbaum’s governing Morena party, according to sources familiar with the talks.
Among the politicians who have faced US scrutiny is Sinaloa Governor Ruben Rocha Moya, who has repeatedly denied wrongdoing.
Sheinbaum added on Friday that “the United States should focus on tackling drug consumption and criminal groups operating within its own territory.”

Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
The proposal comes as President Zelenskyy criticises Trump’s ‘friendship’ with Putin.
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.

“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.
Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.
He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.
Previous attempts at a ceasefire
The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters, and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.
A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.
In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.
International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.
On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.
Friends to foes
The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.
“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.
He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.
After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.
Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

articles.title: Mecca pact allies condemn ‘heinous’ Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

articles.full_text:
Mecca pact allies condemn ‘heinous’ Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Senior officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye pledge to protect the kingdom’s security during talks in Islamabad.
Pakistan and Turkiye have renewed their pledge to support Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its security and sovereignty, as senior government and defence officials from the three countries denounced the continuing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on the kingdom.
The statement followed a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Mecca defence pact countries in the Pakistani capital, Islamabad, on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Can the Mecca pact turn its collective defence promise into real support?
- list 2 of 3Are GCC countries looking for a regional security pact with Iran?
- list 3 of 3Turkiye’s parliament ratifies Mecca defence agreement
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three. The committee comprises the three nations’ foreign and defence ministers alongside top military officials.
Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar thanked the participating officials after the roughly two-and-a-half-hour meeting.
“The SPDC meeting reviewed the evolving regional security situation and reaffirmed the determination of the three countries to continue working collectively towards regional peace, security and stability,” he told reporters.
“The three sides reiterated their strong condemnation of the persistent and heinous attacks by the Houthi militia, targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“They reaffirmed their collective resolve to continue and intensify efforts to support the kingdom in safeguarding its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the collective defence provisions of the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defence.”
Houthi attacks continue
The high-level talks come as Saudi Arabia continues to face attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis, who have repeatedly targeted Saudi cities, oil facilities and shipping since fighting in Yemen intensified in July.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.
These attacks were expected to top Friday’s agenda, but no details were released regarding any concrete measures.
At an emergency meeting of the pact’s members in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.
Pakistan has previously pledged to defend Saudi territory, while ruling out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also told Turkish media last week that Ankara’s current policy was aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia.
“No decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia,” he said.
Dar said Friday’s discussions also focused on implementing decisions made at previous meetings of the alliance, as well as boosting cooperation across various sectors.
“The parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in defence industries, joint technological development, training, and capacity building, with a view to enhancing the collective capabilities and cohesion of their armed forces in order to address mutual security concerns and contribute to peace and security in the region,” he said.
Turkiye’s Fidan said that kind of integration sits at the core of the pact’s strategy.
“The greatest goal of this alliance is for countries here to pool their own capabilities – not only their military capabilities, but also their defence industry capabilities – to generate greater power, create greater impact, and make a larger contribution to peace and stability,” Anadolu news agency quoted him as saying after the meeting.
Fidan also said that ongoing negotiations between the United States and Iran were discussed, while several decisions were made in principle regarding the roadmap to follow for other countries wishing to become members of the alliance.
Several regional nations have already expressed interest in joining the pact. In an August interview with Al Jazeera, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could potentially join the pact.
Bangladesh has also stated it is actively considering joining the agreement, while Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said last month that Damascus is weighing whether to enter the Mecca alliance.

articles.full_text:
Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez makes last bid to beat right-wing parties before Spanish vote on Sunday.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in a snap general election on Sunday, despite adverse public polling suggesting a right-wing advantage.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” the Socialist leader told radio station SER on Friday, as political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning before the vote.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3What you should know about Spain’s election
- list 2 of 3Andalusia offers a glimpse into Spain’s future as far right gains ground
- list 3 of 3What Spain’s election means for Morocco
The outcome of the election will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys within five days of an election, Sanchez insisted that internal data suggested his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.
He said that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Choice between ‘regression and progressivism’
Earlier, during a televised pre-election debate, Sanchez clashed with PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Vox’s Santiago Abascal, as well as Ada Colau, a left-wing Spanish politician and former mayor of Barcelona associated with the Sumar political alliance, in a debate focused on immigration, the housing crisis and foreign policy.
The prime minister criticised the Madrid regional government, controlled by the PP, for awarding an honorary medal to the Israeli government while the assault on Gaza continued.
“It is shameful,” Sanchez said, accusing his opponents of having “no humanity whatsoever.”
He also interrupted Feijoo when the conservative leader described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “massacre”, insisting that “it is genocide”.
Sanchez warned voters that Spain faced a choice between “regression and progressivism”, arguing that the PP and Vox wanted to replicate the politics of US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with Trump and criticism of Israel. The dynamism of the EU’s fourth-largest economy under his leadership has also drawn praise at a turbulent time for global markets.
But a polarising status at home puts his tenure in peril.
‘Day of reflection’
Sanchez is holding his final large rally in Madrid on Friday, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the “regression” of a possible PP-Vox coalition.
“We are unstoppable and we will win!” he told a Socialist meeting in the western city of Plasencia, sporting a red T-shirt emblazoned with the slogan “the power of women”.
He contrasted a Spain “of prosperity, principles and values” against a “reactionary coalition” that would question women’s rights, cut pensions and gut public services.
PP leader Feijoo, who won the most seats at the last election in 2023 but failed to form a government, told supporters in Barcelona: “This time we will pull it off.”
Dismissing Sanchez’s campaign of “fear”, he will hold his campaign finale in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region.
Addressing reporters before a closing rally in the eastern city of Valencia, Vox leader Abascal accused Sanchez’s “mafia-style” government of “betraying, robbing and lying” to the country.
Spaniards will observe a “day of reflection” on the eve of the vote on Saturday. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

articles.title: ‘Bear trap’: Ukraine hails new operation as Russian casualties mount
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Russian assaults met with stout defence along the front as Western powers discuss ceasefire proposals.
articles.full_text:
‘Bear trap’: Ukraine hails new operation as Russian casualties mount
Russian assaults met with stout defence along the front as Western powers discuss ceasefire proposals.
Ukraine’s forces liberated more of their land as Russia broke new casualty records and United States negotiators tried to convince Kyiv to give up territory, or NATO membership.
Details emerged on November 20 of a new operation – the fourth this year – in which Ukraine said it cleared Russian troops out of hundreds of square kilometres of land they occupied, this time in the northern Kharkiv region.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4Ukraine drone attack kills five in Russian-occupied Zaporizhia
- list 2 of 4Why is Italy angry with Ukraine for striking Russian ships off Libya?
- list 3 of 4EU leaders struggle to agree on long-term budget, $49bn Ukraine loan
- list 4 of 4Inside Ukraine’s power crisis amid its war with Russia
That was about a month after Russia said it had encircled 2,000 Ukrainian troops in an enclave adjacent to the Russian border, around the town of Velykyi Burluk.
Ukrainian commanders realised that the troops were in danger of being encircled, and ordered the execution of “Operation Bear Trap”, which relied on deceptive moves and secrecy to attack the enemy from various sides, concealing its main direction.
Ukrainian forces used a Russian T-80 tank and an Abrams M-1 tank to attack the border town of Vilhuvatka, giving the impression that their main blow would land there.
They then attacked Russian reinforcements from the rear as they arrived to shore up defences, and used drones to remotely mine Russian resupply routes.
The Ukrainian command said Operation Bear Trap has so far succeeded in liberating 200sq km (77sq miles) and 14 settlements, and was ongoing.
Russian troops continue to occupy at least four border villages in Kharkiv, including Vovchansk, but their plan to seize almost 500sq km (193sq miles) has been foiled.
It is not the first time Ukrainian forces preempted a Russian pincer movement.
Earlier this year they stopped an attempted encirclement of the “fortress belt” of Sloviansk, Kramatorsk and Druzhivka in the eastern Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi.
But Kyiv still struggled to defend its skies and nationwide power outages are making life miserable for Ukrainians.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces in Donetsk were engaged in active defence, stopping attempted assaults and destroying vehicles.
Retired Ukrainian colonel Konstantyn Mashovets, who analyses the front on his Telegram channel, said Kyiv’s forces had also advanced in southern Zaporizhia, clearing Russian infiltrators out of the northern bank of the Solona river near Novopavlivka.
As Russia continued these assaults, its casualties rose to a record on November 24 of 432,519, Ukraine’s military said. The next day, it set a new monthly record of 55,629 for November, with five days to go in the month.
Despite Ukraine’s battlefield achievements, US mediation offers remained unchanged.
US negotiators had put two proposals before Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported, citing people involved in talks. Both involved an exchange of land for peace.
In one, Ukraine would cede the “fortress belt” of cities in Donetsk and receive full NATO membership, the WSJ said.
But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has rejected the idea of retreating from that well-defended position.
Russian official Dmitry Medvedev reiterated on November 20 that Ukraine’s potential NATO membership was a key reason for the war. He also suggested partitioning Ukraine, proposing that Lviv could be handed to Poland as part of a deal.
“The enemy has not abandoned its goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood,” said Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.
US negotiator Jared Kushner told a Berlin news conference that Russia had accepted a watered-down version of this US proposal – the second option outlined by the WSJ – of creating NATO-style security guarantees for Ukraine in return for freezing the front line.
“We have been able to convince the Russians of this concept that any security guarantees for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “President Trump is open to it, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest.”
It would be in the US interest, as he explained on social media, if “broader security arrangements made it highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked. This is why security guarantees for Ukraine cannot be finalised in isolation from post-war European security architecture.”
It appeared, therefore, that Europe would have to assume the burden of a future defence of Ukraine, something Russia has also rejected, because it refuses to accept European forces on Ukrainian soil.
Those NATO-style guarantees would have to be offered from the safety of NATO soil, rendering them less effective.
Zelenskyy told journalists he did not trust a deal between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom Trump referred to as “my friend” on November 19.
He told Bloomberg the US and Russia were effectively in cahoots to bully Ukraine.
“It’s very unfortunate when, during discussions about how to end the war, Starshield either malfunctions or has limitations, and not only are there fewer missiles for Patriot systems, but there are also other issues that prevent deliveries,” he said.
“Politically, it looks as if [the US] is moving in the same direction as what Putin wants: to force Ukraine into unfavourable compromises,” Zelenskyy said.
Europe did not appear to be in a listening mood any more than Ukraine.
“Russia wants more than Ukraine,” German chancellor Friedrich Merz told parliament. “Russia is escalating in the Baltic. Russia is escalating in Poland. Russia is escalating on the Black Sea. Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is escalating massively here in our own country.”
Merz was referring to two Russian missiles and a Russian drone, which crashed in an area of Poland on November 20, where a multinational force of more than 5,000 personnel from Britain, France, Belgium, Estonia, Spain, the Netherlands, Lithuania, Germany, Poland and Sweden was conducting its first military exercise.
Ukraine made its own response to Russia very clear during the past week.
On November 21 it struck the Sparta II, a Russian logistics vessel en route from St. Petersburg to Kaliningrad.
The next day two Ukrainian naval drones struck and sank the Russian corvette Merkury near the Libyan port of Benghazi, in an attack that has caused tensions between Italy and Ukraine.
“The operation involved 7 unmanned boats manufactured in Ukraine, which were transported to the designated location and launched from a ‘mother ship’,” said the Ukraine Security Force (SBU).
On the same day, Ukraine struck another Russian logistics ship, the Angara, also in the Mediterranean.
Ukraine’s strikes inside Russia also continued.
On November 25, Ukrainian forces attacked the Savasleyka airfield, damaging a Mig-31 and two Sukhoi-24 bombers, all used to launch Khinzal missiles. Three days earlier, Russia had fired 84 cruise missiles into Ukraine.
Ukraine struck the Kaleykino pumping station, which sits on the Druzhba oil pipeline and helps export Russian crude, on November 20 and again on November 23. The strikes reportedly destroyed three 50,000 tonne oil tanks.
During the week Ukraine also struck the Novoshakhtinsk, Permnefteorgsintez, Kuibishevsk, and Sizran refineries, all key to supplying the Russian military. The furthest of these was 3,000km (1,800 miles) from unoccupied Ukraine.
Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries have lowered its refining capacity by an estimated one-third, and caused fuel shortages.
Ukraine’s military intelligence estimated that over the three months ending on October 22, Russia imported almost a million tonnes of refined fuels, including 128,000 tonnes of diesel.

articles.title: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.snippet: Hackers have reportedly breached the service's flagship cloud computing platform, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of tactical, personnel and logistics data.
articles.full_text:
Hackers have breached the U.S. Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.
The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.
In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”
A ONE-STOP SHOP
Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.
Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 U.S. Air Force locations around the world.
SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2025, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.
Cloud One is among the U.S. military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.
“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.
Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the U.S. military’s cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.
Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.
A RANGE OF DISRUPTION
The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.
Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.
All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.
One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.
Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.
STRING OF HACKS
News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.
The U.S. government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.
Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.
In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100% success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.
“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote.

articles.title: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly hacked in latest federal breach
articles.snippet: Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department. [...]
articles.full_text:
Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department.
According to Reuters, the intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates.
Launched in 2017, Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform managed by the US Air Force that allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance.
According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information.
US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown.
The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, telling Reuters that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities.
The reported Air Force breach follows other cybersecurity incidents disclosed over the past week targeting US federal agencies.
On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies.
The database contains information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records.
The intrusion came two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov.
Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA).
Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems.
It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected.
AI-powered hacking tools fuel cyberattacks
The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform, which the FBI recently warned was being used to automate cyberattacks worldwide.
In an advisory, the FBI said multiple threat actors had used ARTEX since at least August 2026 in attacks targeting government, defense, healthcare, financial, and technology organizations.
ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data.
The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention.
According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours.
The platform was used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940 in an October attack targeting ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service. Cybersecurity firm Huntress identified at least 162 compromised Microsoft 365 customer tenants during the campaign.
Other attacks linked to ARTEX include:
- Attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information of approximately 67,000 people.
- A South Korean hacking campaign targeting more than 90 organizations, resulting in the theft of approximately 8.2 million data records and the arrest of seven suspects.
- A cyberespionage campaign attributed by CrowdStrike to a Chinese hacking group tracked as Vapor Panda, which targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries and compromised at least nine.
As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX management consoles, with the number believed to be much higher.
It remains unknown whether ARTEX or other AI-powered hacking tools were used in the attacks against the Air Force, FBI, or FinCEN.
