articles.title: France kicks off defense-industry pact to build up counter-drone efforts
articles.snippet: The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have been a “quite brutal reality check,” and French forces have an urgent need for counter-drone capabilities, said Alice Rufo, France’s junior minister for the armed forces.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — France kicked off an initiative with its defense industry to produce counter-drone systems, a new chapter in efforts to foster a local drone ecosystem through “pacts” with industry that bring together firms and military end users, cut procurement red tape and focus on fast contract delivery.
The new pact adds a counter-drone dimension to France’s existing drone pact and will run to the end of summer 2027, said Emmanuel Levacher, chairman of defense-industry association Gicat and the CEO of military vehicle maker Arquus.
“We then hope it will be renewed while incorporating both drone and counter-drone, the idea being that one does not go without the other,” Levacher told Defense News on Wednesday night, after a presentation of the new counter-drone pact in the offices of semiconductor maker STMicroelectronics, just outside Paris.
The drone pact announced in June 2024 has been an attempt by France to play catch up in tactical drones and loitering munitions, led by the country’s Directorate General for Armament together with Gicat. Following up on the success of the original drone pact, France in November announced a similar pact for naval drones, on the occasion of the Euronaval defense trade show.
The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have been a “quite brutal reality check,” and French forces have an urgent need for counter-drone capabilities, Alice Rufo, France’s junior minister for the armed forces, said in a speech at the presentation. She said France has already faced problems related to having insufficient counter-drone capability, without providing details.
France has faced multiple incidents with drones overflying sensitive military sites, including the Île Longue nuclear submarine base in December 2025 and the Toulon naval base in October this year. French media have also reported drones flying over a Eurenco explosives plant in Bergerac and a freight train carrying Leclerc main battle tanks near Mulhouse in November 2025.
The new pact covers systems to counter unmanned aerial vehicles but also maritime and ground drones, according to Levacher. The Gicat chairman said he expects most or all of the 200 partners in the drone pact to participate in the counter-drone initiative.
The goal of the counter-drone pact is “to really be in contact with the armed forces” to understand their requirements, as well as with the DGA to facilitate testing, validation and orders, Levacher said.
“The idea is really to bring together all the stakeholders to create this cross-pollination, speed, contacts,” Levacher said. “This pact is a way of saying that this is an area that does still need to structure and organize itself a little.”
The drone pact has functioned as a meeting place for industry where companies have been able to find project partners, as well as a forum to share feedback from Ukraine, according to Levacher. The DGA uses the drone pact as a framework for informal calls for ideas.
While the demand, the connections and the ecosystem are primarily French, the drone pact firms also pursue export opportunities, Levacher said.
Within the framework of the drone pact, French startup Harmattan AI won a contract in June 2025 to supply the French Army with 1,000 low-cost drones, which it delivered in January this year ahead of the Orion exercise.

Babb will work alongside Editor-in-Chief J.D. Simkins, who continues to lead coverage by the Military Times and Defense News newsroom. Babb most recently served as national security correspondent for Newsmax and spent more than a decade as Voice of America’s Pentagon correspondent, reaching a global audience of hundreds of millions. She has also reported for Military Times and Defense News.
Babb’s scoops include the 2020 Iranian missile attack on U.S. troops at Iraq’s Al-Asad Air Base, U.S. military interdictions of illicit oil tankers in 2025, and troop deployments and military operations during the 2026 war with Iran. Her interviews with senior military leaders have generated headlines across major national outlets, including The Washington Post, Newsweek, Fox News and NBC News.
“Military Times and Defense News are where service members and their families turn for unvarnished insight and accountability on the issues that shape their lives, and I’m excited about where we can take them next,” said Babb. “I’m eager to get to work with Jon and this newsroom to chase the stories our readers need, widen our coverage and shape national security conversations.”
A prominent advocate for independent defense journalism, Babb serves as vice president of the board of Military Reporters and Editors.
Later this week, Babb will receive the prestigious Prize of Excellence from the Association of Foreign Correspondents in the United States for her outstanding contributions to journalism and distinguished national security reporting. articles.title: Estimates of Russians killed in Ukraine surpass all combined US war deaths since WWI
articles.snippet: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago.
articles.full_text:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the war in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale war against the nation nearly five years ago, according to an updated estimate released on Monday.
Based on analysis of leaked official data by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers from Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat, two Russian opposition outlets, Mediazona and Meduza, have confirmed that, accounting for time lags and troops reported missing in action, Russian fatalities jumped from 490,000 at the end of September to more than 720,000 since the start of the conflict in February 2022.
That number, CNN reports, equates to roughly one death every four minutes. The estimate does not include the number of soldiers wounded.
“We are confident that this data is authentic: it is verified against the list of names of the deceased (including records not yet published), the Register of Inheritance Cases, other leaked records from civil registry offices, the texts of court decisions from open sources, and previously published data from Rosstat itself,” Meduza reported.
The Kremlin has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early start of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu acknowledged that it stood at nearly 6,000. This has left many Russian civilians with perhaps little understanding of the full breadth of the conflict as President Vladimir Putin continues to suppress critical information regarding the war at home.
This grim assessment is particularly stark when placed next to U.S. military casualties. If accurate, the number of Russians dead in Ukraine has surpassed all combined U.S. military deaths since World War I.
According to official DoD numbers — exact death counts vary, with historians often clashing over official counts for years, even decades — the U.S. suffered 116,516 total military deaths in WWI; 405,399 military deaths in WWII; 36,574 military deaths during the Korean War; 58,220 during the Vietnam War; 382 in the Persian Gulf War; 2,459 in Afghanistan; 4,493 in Iraq; and 362 military deaths from conflicts in Grenada, Panama, Somalia and Beirut.
The total, 624,547, spanning over 100 years, still falls far below that of Russia in the past five.
While 700,000 lives lost is staggering, it still pales when compared to Soviet dead after Nazi Germany launched Operation Barbarossa in June 1941. During four years of war, it is estimated that 8.8 million to 10.7 million Soviet soldiers were killed. Combined with civilian deaths, that estimate hovers around the grim figure of 24 million Soviet deaths.

articles.title: US Air Force buys final KC-46 lot under Boeing’s original tanker deal
articles.snippet: The Pentagon announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program's original 2011 contract.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon on Tuesday announced a $2.82 billion Boeing contract for 15 more KC-46A Pegasus tankers, the final production lot under the program’s original 2011 contract.
The deal comes in about $350 million above the previous 15-tanker lot, which the Air Force bought for $2.47 billion a year ago. The earlier lot is expected to be complete by mid-2029 and the new lot by mid-2030, according to the Pentagon.
The Air Force has received 116 KC-46As so far, and 203 are on contract or in service worldwide, Boeing said. Japan and Israel also fly the tanker.
“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, KC-46 program vice president, said in Boeing’s release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”
Tuesday’s award is the last of 13 production lots priced into the original contract, Boeing’s filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission show.
After that, the Air Force plans to buy up to 75 more KC-46As from Boeing through a program called Tanker Production Extension, according to an April contracting notice. The service wants 263 KC-46As for itself, which it says will fully replace its KC-135s, built in the 1950s and early 1960s.
Air Force Vice Chief of Staff Gen. John Lamontagne said the 75-jet buy depends on Boeing fixing some of the tanker’s problems, Reuters reported. He didn’t specifically identify the problems, but the best-known KC-46A issues involve the refueling boom and the Remote Vision System, or RVS, the cameras boom operators use to guide it.
“We are working through a couple of issues with the contractor, and we are not going to get a new contract for another 75 KC-46s until we work through some of those deficiencies,” Lamontagne told a Senate Armed Services subcommittee March 4. He said a decision was likely two years away.
Boeing said in June it had completed the first phase of flight testing on a redesigned RVS 2.0. The Air Force has projected fielding the upgraded system in summer 2027, three years later than originally planned.
The KC-46 program has been costly for Boeing. It built the tanker under a firm-fixed-price contract, which leaves the company to cover cost overruns, and has recorded more than $7 billion in losses, including $565 million late last year that Boeing blamed on higher production costs.
The service has said the main issues keeping KC-46s from being ready to fly are the reliability of the aerial refueling system and parts shortages. In May, the Air Force and Boeing agreed on a plan that, along with funding in the fiscal 2027 budget request, is expected to increase KC-46 availability by more than 20% by 2030.

articles.title: Air Force issues Boeing $2.8 billion for more KC-46s
articles.snippet: The award brings the total number of air refuelers under contract to 203, and is the final production batch for the US Air Force under the program’s original fixed-price contract.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Air Force has awarded Boeing $2.8 billion to build a new batch of KC-46 Pegasus air refuelers, the Pentagon announced.
The award for the aircraft’s 13th production lot covers 15 aircraft, with work expected to wrap up by the end of June 2030, according to the Defense Department contract notice, published Tuesday. The aircraft is manufactured by Boeing at the company’s facilities in Seattle, Wash.
“We’re grateful for the trust the U.S. Air Force continues to place in our team,” Jake Kwasnik, Boeing’s vice president for the KC-46 program, said in a company press release. “The KC-46 plays an important role in enabling military operations around the world, and we look forward to building on that partnership while staying focused on delivering on our commitments to support the warfighter.”
The Tuesday award brings the total number of refuelers under contract to 203, inclusive of foreign sales, according to Boeing. The company says it has so far delivered 116 Pegasus aircraft to the Air Force, as well as six to Japan and two to Israel. And other customers could be on the way, after the US in August cleared a KC-46 sale for Qatar.
The KC-46 is based on Boeing’s 767 commercial jet and is the US’s newest air refueler, which officials are buying to gradually recapitalize a fleet of aging KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft. In addition to gassing up other jets, the Pegasus can move cargo and people similar to other large mobility aircraft.
The Lot 13 award is the final under the program’s original fixed-price contract that kicked off in 2011, where developmental challenges and production woes have driven billions of dollars in losses for Boeing. The Air Force intends to continue the tanker’s production run under a new “extension” program and order up to 75 additional aircraft, which would commence with Lot 14, the service indicated in a previously published document. However, officials have said that future aircraft would come with price jumps.
Air Force officials have also pledged not to move forward with the extension plan unless the jet’s lingering top issues, known as category 1 deficiencies, are resolved. A key planned upgrade will address the aircraft’s troubled vision system that operators use to guide a refueling boom to receiving aircraft. The service expects to field that new remote vision system, dubbed RVS 2.0, beginning in early 2028.
The Air Force is buying more KC-46s as the service evaluates options for a follow-on tanking solution. The service is now launching a new round of analysis for its refueling plans, with an emphasis on enhancing existing aircraft, according to Aviation Week.
But some believe the Air Force needs a fresh approach for its tanker fleet. A recent report by the Hudson Institute recommended that officials should buy newly designed air refuelers — in this case, a blended-wing body aircraft — to provide greater range and fuel offload. The report’s authors argue that this new aircraft would be better suited for conflict with China.

articles.title: Delivery of first MV-75 for testing officially delayed amid funding setbacks: Army
articles.snippet: A funding shortfall disrupted communications between the Army and Bell, pushing the service past its original delivery target as officials work to establish a revised schedule.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army will not meet its initial goal of receiving the first MV-75 tiltrotor long-range assault helicopter for testing by the end of this year, according to the service’s acquisition shop.
“Delivery of the MV-75 for testing will not occur by the end of 2026. The program made deliberate efforts toward this goal while making measurable program progress,” a spokesperson from the Army Acquisition, Logistics and Technology (ASA(ALT)) office told Breaking Defense on Nov. 20.
“The Army remains on a path to complete development and testing in approximately half the time of comparable historical programs,” they added.
In January, then-Army Chief Gen. Randy George said the service expected to accept an airframe for testing by the end of 2026. But a subsequent funding shortfall disrupted communications between the Army and Bell — the program’s prime contractor — contributing to the missed delivery target.
The Army has not yet determined when it will receive the first aircraft for testing, the ASA(ALT) spokesperson said. The service is working with Bell, a subsidiary of Textron, “to develop an updated, resource-loaded integrated schedule and schedule risk analysis to establish achievable milestones at an affordable cost,” they added.
Bell was selected as the prime contractor for the MV-75 Cheyenne II tiltrotor in late 2022. Developed under the Army’s Future Long Range Assault Aircraft program, the Army has said the Cheyenne will fly “twice as fast” and “twice as far” as any of the service’s existing assault helos. It’s also set to gradually replace at least some of the service’s UH-60 Black Hawk fleet once fielded.
The missed delivery target follows a funding shortfall that emerged earlier this year after the Army spent nearly all of its available fiscal 2026 funding for the MV-75 by July, according to Textron’s latest quarterly filing. The company continued work on the program while reducing spending to manage the funding shortfall, the report stated.
In July, the Army requested to shift $350 million in funding to the MV-75 program to support the company’s work building and testing eight prototype tiltrotor aircraft. Congress approved that reprogramming request during the third quarter, as Breaking Defense previously reported.
About $300 million was committed to the program in contract changes, covering costs the company and its suppliers had already incurred, Textron CEO Lisa Atherton said in October during an earnings call with investors.
According to the ASA(ALT) spokesperson, Bell “chose to continue certain activities at its own risk without additional funding.” Both the company and the Army said communications between the two halted during the funding gap and did not resume until Sept. 28 when the service received the reprogrammed funding.
“Once funding was received, normal contract execution and communications resumed. The funding gap affected the planned schedule; the Army and Bell are now assessing those effects and updating the program schedule and risk analysis to establish realistic, affordable milestones and delivery dates,” the spokesperson said. “As we restart, the focus is on disciplined execution with a risk-informed path ahead that fits within the available budget.”
Separately, uncertainty surrounding the fiscal 2027 budget could further complicate the program’s timeline. The Army requested more than $2 billion for the MV-75 program in FY27, all of which under discretionary spending, but delays in approving that funding could push back the aircraft’s first low-rate initial production (LRIP) contract, as Breaking Defense previously reported.
“With the start of the fiscal year in a [continuing resolution], we’d expect a possible push in the timing of the LRIP award. Previously, we were thinking Q4 into Q1 of next year,” Chief Financial Officer David Rosenberg said during the October earnings call.
Though the program has faced delays, Army Undersecretary Michael Obadal told Breaking Defense in a statement that the service still considers the aircraft a “priority” and is committed to delivering the aircraft to soldiers as soon as possible.
“Getting the MV-75 into hands of Army aviators will be the culmination of one of the biggest Army acquisitions. The Cheyenne meets the endurance and close combat demands of large-scale combat operations,” he said. “It extends the distance over which commanders can deliver, reinforce, and reposition assault forces. It’s a priority for the joint force.”
The delay in the aircraft’s delivery for testing, along with the potential LRIP delay, follows uncertainty over the MV-75 program’s schedule. During a call with reporters in April, Maj. Gen. Clair Gill, then the Program Acquisition Executive for Maneuver Air, declined to commit to dates for the aircraft’s first flight or start of production.
“It’s going to happen when it’s going to happen. So we are moving as fast as we can,” Gill said at the time. “If I was king, and I had all the money in the world and all the engineers, and there were no limits, we probably would be able to do it in a matter of months.”

articles.title: NATO sees no Russian naval buildup in the Med after strike near Libya, but analysts warn of wider risks
articles.snippet: Experts say Ukraine’s strike could have consequences far beyond Libya, raising the risk of Russian retaliation and heightened tensions along NATO’s southern flank.
articles.full_text:
MILAN — While NATO does not anticipate a Russian naval buildup in the Mediterranean after a recent Ukrainian drone strike near Libya, the operation has raised concerns about the risk of drawing the North African country deeper into the war and threatening the alliance’s southern flank.
Ukraine used unmanned vessels to strike two Russian ships near the Libyan port of Benghazi along the Mediterranean coast on Sunday, sinking a warship and damaging a cargo vessel, according to the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU). Despite questions about the potential for a wider response from Moscow, NATO “is not expecting a surge or redeployment of further Russian assets in the Mediterranean,” an alliance official told Breaking Defense.
That is largely because the Russian surface fleet “is having serious war-generation issues,” according to the NATO official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
The alliance is more concerned about the conflict spilling over into other areas and the potential for attacks on commercial shipping, both in the Mediterranean and elsewhere, the official said. Such attacks, they added, have already been seen in the Black Sea, where Russia has targeted “innocent merchant shipping.”
NATO routinely evaluates its force posture and readiness in the [Mediterranean] region, the official added. They noted that on any given day, the average “ratio of NATO deployed assets to those of Russia is 3:1” — meaning that for every one Russian surface ship, there are three allied surface ships underway. That imbalance is even greater in the Mediterranean, where the alliance’s deployed assets outnumber Russia’s by roughly 5-6 to 1, the official added.
Although NATO does not anticipate an immediate shift in the Russian naval presence, questions remain about how Kyiv conducted the operation and what it could mean for the region.
Earlier this year, the Associated Press reported that Libyan officials said Ukrainian forces, most of them drone specialists, had been operating from military facilities in western Libya. The officials, who spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity, identified an air base in Misrata as the main site, along with facilities in Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya.
Libyan officials briefed on Sunday’s attack also told the AP that the Russian corvette was struck at the Benghazi Naval Base, claiming that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the vessel.
The Ukrainian SBU, meanwhile, said the seven naval drones were delivered to a designated location and launched into the water from a “mothership” near the target. The agency did not identify the vessel or specify where the drones were launched, leaving questions about whether the operation originated from Libyan territory.
Deep divisions remain across the North African country following the 2011 overthrow of the Muammar Gaddafi regime and the subsequent civil wars that erupted. The western part of Libya, largely centered around Tripoli, is controlled by the UN-recognized Government of National Unity (GNU), formed in 2021 and led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh.
Meanwhile, eastern Libya is controlled by rival authorities aligned with military commander Khalifa Haftar and his Libyan National Army (LNA). The area shares close ties to Moscow, as authorities have allowed Russian naval vessels to use the port of Tobruk as a resupply and refueling hub.
According to Arturo Varvelli, head of the Rome office and senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, it remains unclear whether Ukraine launched its attack from western Libya, as the claim has not yet been independently verified, even by Moscow. However, he warned that the operation could have serious ripple effects for the region and possibly draw the war in Ukraine closer to NATO’s southern flank.
“The United Nations’ mission has already called for an independent investigation, warning against the risk of dragging Libya into foreign conflicts,” Varvalli told Breaking Defense. “This is precisely the greatest strategic danger: that Libya could turn into yet another theater of the war between Russia and Ukraine, just a few hundred kilometers from Italy.”
He referred to statements by Aydar Aganin, Moscow’s ambassador to Libya, who was quoted by Russian state media outlet RT as saying the attack “will not go unanswered” and that Moscow is weighing its options. While Varvelli assesses that an armed retaliation against western Libya is unlikely in the immediate future, an asymmetric response is more probable.
“Eastern authorities have stated that Libya ‘reserves the right to respond by all necessary means’; however, I believe a direct kinetic response against western Libya is unlikely in the short term, as the costs for both sides would be extremely high,” he said.
One potential complication for Moscow is the presence of foreign military personnel in Misrata, where Ukraine’s main base is reportedly located at the Air Force Academy. The coastal city in northwestern Libya is aligned with the UN-backed GNU, and the facility is reportedly shared with Turkish and Italian forces, US Africa Command (AFRICOM) and a British intelligence center.
“An attack by Russia or the Libyan National Army [governed by Haftar] on Misrata would risk striking Turkish, Italian or US personnel present in the area,” Varvelli said. “Asymmetric responses are more likely. … Consequently, any retaliation might more simply be directed against Kyiv.”
Italy has maintained a military presence in the western part of the country since 2018 through its Bilateral Mission of Assistance and Support in Libya (MIASIT).
Vincenzo Camporini, Italy’s former chief of defense general staff, also raised concerns about potential Russian retaliation. In an interview published Monday by Italian media Agenzia Nova, Camporini warned that if Moscow retaliated against western Libya — possibly by encouraging LNA forces to act — it could risk reigniting a civil war inside the country, only this time with greater direct involvement from Russia and Turkey.
On Tuesday, the GNU’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation stated that Libya’s territory would not be used as a staging ground for attacks and referred to the strike in Benghazi as highlighting “the danger of hosting foreign forces that operate outside the authority of the state.”
Kyiv has also pushed back against suggestions that it is expanding the war beyond Ukraine. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on his Telegram channel on Tuesday that “Ukraine is not ‘dragging’ anyone into the war or ‘transferring’ the war anywhere.”

articles.title: Israel increases defense budget by $5 billion as concerns continue over future funding
articles.snippet: Israel has scrambled several times this year to increase its defense spending, at the cost of other priorities.
articles.full_text:
JERUSALEM — Israel’s Joint Committee on the Defense Budget has approved a $5 billion increase to Israel’s defense budget, despite the ongoing uncertainty about who will be prime minister in the wake of the country’s Oct. 27 elections, and budget challenges nationwide.
Israel Katz, the country’s defense minister, said that he welcomed the decision by the committee “to approve an addition of approximately NIS 17.3 billion to the 2026 defense budget, as part of the initiative I led to strengthen the IDF’s capabilities and build up its forces for the coming years.”
He added that the approval will enable Israel to “advance plans for blue-and-white self-reliance in long-term procurement in space, attack helicopters, air defense, and other classified areas.”
The term “blue and white,” the colors of the Israeli flag, refers to an effort by Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to make Israel more independent in defense production by investing heavily in local companies and products.
However, the spending increase will only do so much to shore up defense plans in the wake of budget shortfalls that will stretch into 2027.
In March 2026, Israel approved a record defense budget of $45 billion, but it has continued to receive supplemental spending, including a transfer in August of around $300 million, a $5 billion increase in September and an October deal to fund Apache helicopter purchases. It would appear that Tuesday’s committee decision would bring the defense budget to around $55 billion. These increases were funded by moving money from one part of the approved budget, like from the Ministries of Transport, National Security and Education, among others, to the defense ministry.
At the time, Israeli Ministry of Defense Director General Amir Baram said the Apache deal was made possible due to “creative solutions we developed together with our American partners,” without elaborating on what that means. He did note that the ministry was working to sign more agreements for unnamed “platforms, munitions, interceptors, and more. This is to ensure immediate readiness for any scenario, alongside the implementation of the decade-long force buildup plan, as part of the IMOD’s strategy in the face of emerging challenges.”
In addition, Israel appears to be in debt to its own state-run defense giants, Israel Aerospace Industries and Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.
On Nov. 12, IAI announced its third quarter financial results. In its statement it noted that “as of September 30, 2026, the Israeli Ministry of Defense’s outstanding debt to Israel Aerospace Industries amounts to billions of shekels and is reflected in the company’s financial results. Israel Aerospace Industries calls on the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Finance to urgently reach an agreement to settle this outstanding debt.”
Rafael has not released a statement about the debt issue, although Israel’s Calcalist publication said in October that the debt is around $2.3 billion to Rafael and around $2 billion to IAI.
The budget challenges will seemingly continue into the new year, especially following the announced end of US military aid. It is unclear, however, when or how that will go into effect.
In addition, the new Knesset in Israel is now led by the opposition, even though the opposition has not been able to form a new government. If this situation continues it will also affect the budget discussion in 2027.
“We will continue to act decisively to ensure Israel’s military superiority and give the IDF the tools it needs to protect our citizens and prevail in every arena,” Katz said.

articles.title: First Dark Eagle hypersonic battery ‘fully fielded,’ Lozano says
articles.snippet: Though the three-star would not share when the first battery was fully fielded, the news comes after the program has faced years of delays.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Army has officially fielded its first Long Range Hypersonic Weapon battery, according to the service’s top general in charge of munitions.
“It is fully fielded. It is ready to go,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, Program Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Fires, told Breaking Defense on Nov. 19 during an interview. “It is a global deployable and employable warfighting capability. Those soldiers and those units have everything that they need to employ, fight and win.”
Lozano declined to disclose when or where the first battery was fielded, offering few details about the milestone beyond confirming that the weapon is operational and ready for deployment.
The news comes after years of challenges with developing and fielding the LHRW, also known as the Dark Eagle. The Army initially planned to field the first battery in 2023, but testing woes — including a mechanical engineering problem with the launcher — prevented the service from meeting that goal. The Army later pushed its fielding target to September 2025, but missed that deadline as well.
According to a recent report from Bloomberg, the Army had still not completely fielded its first LRHW battery as of October 2026 — putting the service nearly three years behind schedule. The Army’s program office reportedly said in a statement to Bloomberg at the time that it “continues fielding activities” for the Dark Eagle and must undergo more training and other sustainment and readiness work “before declaring the system fully fielded.”
When asked if the report from October was inaccurate, Lozano said he didn’t “want to go so far as to say that.” Instead, he said “this is a rapidly evolving space, and things can happen very quickly, and for all the right reasons, we in the Army and we at PAE [Program Acquisition Executive] Fires are being very, very aggressive about producing, developing and fielding new capabilities that include Dark Eagle.”
Asked when the first battery officially reached full fielding status, Lozano pointed to the fact that some of the weapon’s ground support equipment had been delivered as early as 2021, making it difficult to identify a specific date for the milestone.
Hypersonic Capabilities
Hypersonic missiles can fly at speeds of Mach 5 or greater and are designed to maneuver unpredictably through the Earth’s atmosphere. Over the past several years, both the Pentagon and Congress have shown a growing interest in developing and acquiring such systems, especially as reports have circulated that Russia and China have a number of hypersonic weapons programs in their arsenals.
The Army’s Dark Eagle program was developed alongside the Navy’s Conventional Prompt Strike project. The weapons have the same glide body system, but the Army will integrate it onto ground launchers. The Navy will launch theirs from Zumwalt-class destroyers and Virginia-class submarines once fielded.
One Dark Eagle consists of four trailer-mounted transporter erector launchers, each carrying two all-up rounds plus canisters, along with a battery operations center and support vehicle.
The Army and Navy chose to pause production while addressing problems identified during testing, according to a Government Accountability Office report from July. Further, the GAO report found that “the contractor [Lockheed Martin] has continued to experience issues at its facility.” This has resulted in “missing, inconsistent, and unclear work standards for missile production.”
Lozano declined to provide further details about manufacturing issues, but said preventing similar problems in the future would require more rigorous qualification testing of individual missile components.
That includes “making sure we test all the solid rocket motors, so that we have a high level of confidence that those things work and perform as required, making sure we’re testing and checking out the integrated guidance sections, making sure we’re testing out and qualifying the inertial [navigation] units [and] making sure we’re testing seeker and seeker components,” he said.
Though Lozano declined to comment on where the battery was fielded, Breaking Defense previously reported that soldiers within the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force long-range fires battalion, 5th Battalion, 3rd Field Artillery Regiment at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in Washington received system components and training in anticipation of becoming that first operational unit with the new weapon in 2023.
The Army is now working to field the second and third batteries, though Lozano could not speculate when they would be ready due to operational security concerns. The service is “already over halfway through production” of the third battery, he noted.
“I don’t have a firm date on the wall, I think we’ll see that the second battery and the third battery will realize their full capability at a faster pace and a faster rate than the first battery did,” he said.
New Companies Incoming?
Separately, Lozano indicated the Army could eventually open the LRHW program to additional vendors, potentially introducing more competition that could offer better performing capabilities at a lower cost.
“I’d like to have two or three vendors all in production against a singular requirement, because then that gives me a lot of production flexibility and options,” he said. “Should any one vendor have any kind of quality or production or manufacturing challenge in delivering, it gives me options to kind of maybe buy more or less from one of the vendors over another.”
Lozano said the Army is also pursuing hypersonic weapons that would fill the capability gap between Dark Eagle and shorter-range systems like Castelion’s Blackbeard hypersonic missile through the “scaled hypersonics program.”
The Dark Eagle uses a land-based truck system to fire rounds capable of traveling over 3,800 miles per hour towards targets within a 1,725-mile range. The Blackbeard has a shorter range, smaller form factor and is cheaper. Therefore, platforms discovered through the scaled hypersonics program would ideally have a range between the Blackbeard and Dark Eagle.
“All of our long-range fires efforts and capabilities are significantly important to the Army and to the Department of [Defense], and so they all remain a very high priority for us,” Lozano said.

articles.title: Japan’s education ministry discloses breach of government procurement system
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Japan’s education ministry disclosed earlier this week that hackers breached its government procurement system, potentially exposing records containing business information and email addresses.
articles.full_text:
Japan’s education ministry discloses breach of government procurement system
Japan’s education ministry disclosed earlier this week that hackers had breached its government procurement system, potentially exposing records containing business information and email addresses.
The Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) said it detected the intrusion on October 1, nearly two months before publicly disclosing the incident. An investigation found that hackers may have obtained information stored in the system’s database.
The potentially compromised data includes nearly 1,700 email addresses and 164,000 records containing company names, the names of employees and other business information, the ministry said in a statement Wednesday.
The affected system is used to publish information about government tenders, contracts and procurement opportunities. The potentially exposed business information relates to companies eligible to participate in the ministry’s bidding processes.
The ministry said it had blocked all communications between the affected system and internal and external networks and found no evidence that the potentially compromised information has been publicly disclosed or misused.
The incident was reported to Japan’s data protection authorities, and the ministry is continuing its investigation in coordination with relevant government agencies. It has not publicly identified the perpetrators or disclosed how they gained access to its systems.
“We will continue to investigate the incident in close cooperation with the relevant authorities and take appropriate action,” MEXT said.
This is the latest cybersecurity incident affecting major Japanese companies and public institutions in recent months.
Earlier this week, Japanese railway operator Keio Corporation said a ransomware attack in September may have compromised the personal information of more than 11 million customers, business partners, employees and job applicants. The ransomware group Qilin, believed to have Russian origins, claimed responsibility for the attack.
McDonald’s Japan also recently disclosed a breach involving a database linked to its official mobile app. The compromised information included customers’ purchase histories, IP addresses, internal customer identification numbers and mobile device location data.
Earlier this month, the city of Osaka disclosed that a breach involving a third-party technology provider had exposed more than 1 million email addresses associated with an online platform for municipal services.
Other major Japanese companies that have reported cybersecurity incidents in recent months include telecommunications giant KDDI, the Japanese unit of U.S. insurer Aflac, electronics manufacturer Nidec and brewer Sapporo Holdings. There is no indication that these incidents are connected.

articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: German software giant SAP confirmed a cybersecurity incident following reports that hackers infiltrated its software development infrastructure, potentially gaining access to the company’s source code.
articles.full_text:
Software giant SAP confirms cyber incident amid reports of source code breach
German software giant SAP confirmed a cybersecurity incident following reports that hackers infiltrated its software development infrastructure, potentially gaining access to the company’s source code.
In a statement to Recorded Future News on Friday, SAP said it had identified suspicious activity and immediately taken steps to protect its customers and secure its services. The company did not disclose the nature or extent of the intrusion.
“Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data,” SAP said. “We will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.”
German magazine Der Spiegel first reported the incident Thursday, citing internal company communications and sources familiar with the matter.
According to the magazine, hackers targeted SAP’s software development environment hosted on GitHub, obtaining employee authentication tokens that allowed them to copy and modify the company’s source code.
The German Press Agency (dpa), which independently reviewed portions of internal SAP communication, reported that the company had alerted employees to suspicious activity within its GitHub environment several days before the incident became public. Employees were advised to assess whether they needed to change their login credentials or take additional security precautions.
SAP launched an internal incident response operation code-named “Project Granite,” according to German business newspaper Handelsblatt.
The company’s emergency security measures reportedly affected several software development teams. SAP restricted access to GitHub, halted automated development processes and replaced digital keys used to verify that its software was genuine and had not been tampered with.
It remains unclear whether the hackers accessed SAP’s proprietary source code or whether any altered code ended up in software delivered to customers.
SAP has not publicly identified who was behind the attack, how the hackers gained access to its systems or whether the incident has been fully contained.
SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software companies whose products are used by businesses and public institutions worldwide to manage critical operations, including accounting, procurement, supply chains and human resources.
The incident follows a separate software supply chain attack in April, when hackers injected malicious code into several open-source software packages developed by SAP in an attempt to steal sensitive information from developers and automated software development environments. It is unclear whether the two incidents are connected.

articles.title: Cyberattack disrupts global news distribution platform at France’s AFP
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: French international news agency Agence France-Presse was hit by a cyberattack Thursday, forcing it to take offline one of its main platforms for distributing news content to media organizations worldwide.
articles.full_text:
Cyberattack disrupts global news distribution platform at France’s AFP
French international news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP) was hit by a cyberattack Thursday, forcing it to take offline one of its main platforms for distributing news content to media organizations worldwide.
The attack targeted AFP Forum, an online platform that news outlets use to browse and download the agency’s stories, photographs and videos.
AFP confirmed the incident Thursday in an internal email to employees, which was quoted in the agency’s own reporting. The agency is investigating the attack with assistance from external cybersecurity experts.
“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” AFP management said in the email.
“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”
The agency is offering subscribers alternative ways to access its content while the platform remains offline, according to French media reports.
AFP Forum remained inaccessible as of Friday, displaying a maintenance notice in several languages. The agency has not identified who was behind the attack or provided a timeline for restoring the service.
It remains unclear whether the hackers gained access to sensitive information or whether other AFP systems were affected.
The agency did not respond to a request for comment.
AFP is one of the world’s three major international news agencies, alongside Reuters and the Associated Press. It traces its roots to Agence Havas, founded in 1835, and took its current name in 1944. It employs more than 1,800 journalists and has 210 bureaus worldwide.
This is not the first cyberattack to disrupt the agency’s content distribution services.
In September 2024, AFP detected a cyberattack on its IT systems that disrupted some of the services used to deliver news content to subscribers. The attack has not been publicly attributed to any hacking group.

articles.full_text:
British government takes services offline following ‘cyber incident’
Britain’s Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said Friday that it had experienced a cyber incident, with several services taken down as a precaution.
The nature of the incident has not been disclosed. In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for the DWP said the department had “taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution following a cyber incident.”
The department is the largest in the British government by spending and administers the state pension and a range of other benefits. Millions of people in the country depend on its payments for essential bills.
“Regular benefit and pension payments are not affected and will be paid as normal,” the spokesperson added.
The department said it was “working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible to minimise any disruption.”
The incident comes days after the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said it has observed “a marked rise” since September in cyberattacks assisted by artificial intelligence.
Earlier this year, the British government acknowledged its yearslong approach to its own cybersecurity was flawed and warned it will be impossible to meet a previous target of securing all government organizations from known cyber vulnerabilities and attack methods by 2030.
“To protect our critical national infrastructure, defend public institutions and maintain public confidence in essential public services, we must achieve a radical shift in approach and a step change in pace,” it said at the time, warning the public sector faced a “critically high” cyber risk.

is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: UK’s long-awaited National Cyber Action Plan delayed until December
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Officials, who had planned to publish the document in mid-November, now aim to unveil the strategy for defending the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hackers on December 9.
articles.full_text:
UK’s long-awaited National Cyber Action Plan delayed until December
Britain has again delayed the launch of its National Cyber Action Plan, the government’s long-awaited strategy for defending the wider economy against state-backed and criminal hackers, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.
The document, originally conceived as a national cyber strategy, was first due to be published by the end of 2025. After initial delays it was rebranded as an action plan and was close to publication in July this year before being postponed amid Keir Starmer’s resignation.
Officials, who had planned to publish the document in mid-November, now aim to unveil it on December 9 according to several sources, speaking to Recorded Future News on condition of anonymity.
The reasons for the latest delay are unclear. A government spokesperson declined to comment on the timing but said ministers remained committed to publishing the plan.
The latest delay follows an influential cross-party House of Lords committee warning that the government “appears complacent” about “potentially catastrophic risks,” including cyberattacks from Russia, China and Iran.
In a report published last week, the National Resilience Committee found Britain was dangerously underprepared for crises which could cascade across the economy, with disruption spilling over multiple sectors and disrupting the everyday lives of millions of people.
Baroness Northover, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, told Recorded Future News that the country could not afford more uncertainty or drift. “This situation is unacceptable at a time of significant and escalating risk,” she said. “We must act urgently. The cost of inaction is enormous.”
“Further absence of an overarching National Cyber Action Plan, aimed at defending the economy against state-backed and criminal hacking, is not just frustrating, it is serious,” she said.
“The UK has got to keep pace with threats. Delay and avoidance is simply not an option and underlines the Committee’s point that the UK remains seriously exposed and underprepared for very significant events, and our vulnerability is current, active and acute on many fronts.”
No dither but delay
Successive delays to cybersecurity legislation and policy announcements have contributed to a perception that the issue is a low political priority, despite its growing importance to Britain’s economic and national security.
The Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, an update to the country's critical-infrastructure cyber laws, took more than four years to reach Parliament and is now not expected to be enforced until 2028 — a decade on from the NIS Regulations it was written to replace.
The core provisions of the CSRB had already been completed back in 2022 under Rishi Sunak, whose government incorrectly described the laws as “updated” before failing to include them in that year's King's Speech setting out the government’s parliamentary agenda and leaving the draft bill ultimately unintroduced to parliament.
When Starmer's government first moved to bring the bill forward in September 2025, it was then delayed again amid a cabinet reshuffle.
Separately, a set of ransomware proposals — mandatory reporting for all victims, a licensing regime for extortion payments and a ban on ransoms for critical infrastructure operators — was due to go out to consultation in mid-2024, before being scuppered when Sunak called a general election.
Officials argue that the delays belie the substantial amount of work underway in Westminster.
The government is expected to bring forward a new National Security Bill next year to reform the Computer Misuse Act — although some fear the reforms as proposed would fail to protect security researchers — as well as finally set the ransomware proposals on the statute books.
In last month’s budget, the government committed £120 million ($159 million) over four years to the AI Security Institute and a further £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit to address the threats posed by AI agents acting autonomously.
Another £70 million ($93 million) was earmarked for an AI-powered vulnerability hunting center at the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), with £60 million ($79 million) allocated to the first phase of Cyber Shield, a national defense system that would use AI agents to find and fix security weaknesses across government and critical infrastructure networks.
Potentially more consequential for the technology industry was a commitment, buried among the budget announcements, that the government would consult next year on “where liability for cyber breaches should sit.”
Ministers have also launched a voluntary Cyber Resilience Pledge, seeking commitments from British businesses to put cybersecurity on the boardroom agenda and better manage their supply-chain risks. The government describes the pledge as a central pillar of the National Cyber Action Plan.
National Cyber Action Plan
The plan’s contents have not been officially disclosed. Recorded Future News understands it will include three pillars focusing on Threat, Growth and Resilience.
The clearest public indication of the government’s approach came in a lecture to the Royal United Services Institute in June by the NCSC’s chief executive Richard Horne.
Horne called for a full court press across what he termed the “near, mid and far spaces” of cyberspace — a framing people familiar with the plan expect to shape the areas it focuses on.
He defined the near space as the defense of individual organizations, the far space as offensive action against adversaries and the “mid space” as the shared “cloud, technology and telecommunications infrastructure,” most of which he said was “in private hands.”
In that space, he said, the government would partner with providers to “harden the mid space and disrupt attacker activity.”
The idea of an action plan is to specifically set out how and when specific activities will be undertaken, rather than simply describing the overall strategy. Sources who spoke to Recorded Future News says the critical details would be in the plan’s implementation schedule.

is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
articles.snippet: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use "advanced cryptographic tools" to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
articles.full_text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.
In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.
“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”
The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.
“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”
Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.
“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”
The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.
Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.
In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.snippet: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
articles.full_text:
At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.
Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.
“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”
Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”
“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”
Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.
One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.
Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.
“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”
Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.
“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”
How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.
The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.
“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”
Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.
Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.
Using an A/B testing platform as the delivery mechanism is a genuinely uncomfortable escalation: the tool that decides which visitors see which experience was never modeled as a malware distribution channel, so none of the usual detections fire. The operational discipline angle is what stands out – attackers versioning and measuring payloads like product features means defenders need the same rigor about what their third-party tags are allowed to change. Supply-chain reviews for marketing stacks rarely get the scrutiny payments or auth integrations do; this will change that.

articles.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
articles.snippet: The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world's most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
articles.full_text:
The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).
Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.
The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.
The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.
Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].
Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.
The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.
Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.
A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.
That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.
More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.
Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.
